newsitem.title: USA: Fed to watch payment system risk - Atlanta's Guynn.
newsitem.headline: Fed to watch payment system risk - Atlanta's Guynn.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta President Jack Guynn said on Wednesday that the U.S. central bank will watch for risks associated with new developments in the nation's payment system.
Guynn stressed that the Fed will continue to uphold the public interest in the functioning of the payment system and regards that duty as an important responsibility of the U.S. central bank.
"We'll be watchers, interested watchers," Guynn told a panel of the Bank Administration Institute (BAI) on the national payments system.
The panel discussed the risks that may be associated with the arrival in the payment system of non-bank financial institutions that create electronic money or handle financial transactions.

"People who will survive in that business will be those who act responsively," Guynn said, adding that the Fed is "concerned about the risks introduced into the payments system by non-financial players."
Elliott McEntee, president of the National Automated Clearing House Association, said he does not expect changes in the payment system to affect settlements anytime soon.
McEntee reminded the audience that financial transactions involve three steps -- authorization, clearing and settlement.
"Regarding settlements, banks have the monopoly and I don't see that changing unless some legislation allows non-banks access to the Fed's settlement system or to the discount window," McEntee said.
The Atlanta Fed president stressed, "It's not necessarily a matter of control," but the Fed will "want to continue to have a public-interest role.
"We are all going to be very careful about the risks involved with these new alliances," Guynn said.
"We (the Fed) still run the payments system in the country and it is, and will remain, an important part of our responsibilities," he said.
John McDonnell, president of Transaction Network Service, said, "The Internet is not ready for prime time."
McDonnell, referring to the Internet as a potential medium for financial transactions, said, "It's a far cry from being able to reliably conduct financial transactions."
McDonnell said this may happen a few years down the road, but "whether the Internet will continue to be free is a question that remains to be answered."
